beats.say: When a question gives you a table of values, Desmos can plot the points and find the equation that fits them. This is called a regression.

card.text: A table of values becomes a graph

beats.say: You type a tilde sign to ask for a regression. Desmos then reports the best fitting constants, and you match them against the answer choices.
We will work through three examples, from an easy one to a hard one, and you will see every step.
Easy example. A table has the points one comma three, two comma five, and three comma seven. Plot them and describe the pattern.
Open a fresh graph. We will create a table with two columns, one for x and one for y.
Desmos creates the table, and each row appears as a point on the graph.
Click a point to read it. The point two comma five is the middle one.
The three points fall on a straight line. The y values go up by two every time x goes up by one, so the slope is two.
Medium example. A table shows x equals one to five, and y equals three, five, seven, nine, eleven. Which linear equation models the data?
We will enter the table and then ask Desmos for a linear regression.
Create the table with x values one to five, and y values three, five, seven, nine, and eleven.
Type y sub one, a tilde, then m times x sub one plus b. Press the right arrow after each subscript to leave it.
Desmos reports m equals two and b equals one. So the data fits y equals two x plus one exactly, and that is the model to pick.
Hard example. A table shows x equals one to five, and y equals three, eight, fifteen, twenty-four, thirty-five. The growth is not constant. Find the quadratic model.
The differences between the y values are five, seven, nine, and eleven, which keep growing. That tells us a quadratic model is more likely than a line.
Create the table with the five x values and the five y values.
For a quadratic regression, type y sub one, a tilde, then a x sub one squared plus b x sub one plus c. Use the right arrow after each subscript and exponent.
Desmos reports a equals one, b equals two, and c equals zero. So the model is y equals x squared plus two x. Check: when x is three, nine plus six is fifteen.
To recap. Add a table, and Desmos plots every row as a point so you can see the pattern.
Type a tilde to run a regression, using the form that matches the pattern: a line, or a quadratic.
Match the reported constants to the answer choices. That completes the Desmos basics. Next, we begin the Math topics with linear equations in one variable.
